name: Adoni-Besek
title: Canaanite ruler in Bezek
summary: Adoni-Besek was a Canaanite ruler in the city of Bezek mentioned at the beginning of Judges. After Joshua's death, the Israelites sought the Lord's guidance on who should lead the fight against the Canaanites, and Judah was chosen. Together with the tribe of Simeon, they defeated Adoni-Besek in a battle at Bezek. This ruler was notorious for his brutal treatment of his enemies – he had ordered seventy defeated kings to have their thumbs and big toes cut off and forced them to gather food scraps under his table. After his defeat, Adoni-Besek himself suffered the same mutilation. His acknowledgment is remarkable: "Seventy kings with cut-off thumbs and big toes gathered food under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." These words show that even a pagan ruler could recognize the true God's just retribution. Adoni-Besek was then taken to Jerusalem, where he died. The story opens Judges and establishes a central theme in the book: God's sovereign control of history and his righteous judgment over the wickedness of the Canaanites.

keyEvents.title: Judah and Simeon's campaign against Bezek
keyEvents.description: After Joshua's death, the Israelites sought the Lord's will on who should go up first against the Canaanites. The Lord appointed Judah, who allied with his brother Simeon. Together they attacked the city of Bezek and defeated an army of ten thousand men.

keyEvents.title: Adoni-Besek defeated and captured
keyEvents.description: The tribes of Judah and Simeon met Adoni-Besek in Bezek and fought against him and his forces of Canaanites and Perizzites. Adoni-Besek fled from the battlefield but was pursued and taken captive.

keyEvents.title: Mutilation and acknowledgment of divine justice
keyEvents.description: The Israelites cut off the thumbs and big toes of Adoni-Besek—the same treatment he had inflicted on his defeated enemies. Adoni-Besek openly acknowledged that God had repaid him justly, admitting that seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off had gathered food under his table.

keyEvents.title: Adoni-Besek's death in Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Adoni-Besek was brought to Jerusalem by the Israelites, where he died. His fate underscores the biblical principle of divine retribution.

versions.summary: Adoni-Besek was a Canaanite king who ruled the city of Bezek. He was known for his cruelty toward defeated kings, cutting off their thumbs and big toes. He himself was defeated by the tribes of Judah and Simeon and suffered the same fate he had inflicted on others, which he acknowledged as God's just retribution.
versions.title: Canaanite king in Bezek
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Canaanite King in Bezek' is good and precise, but it is worth noting that the Bible does not explicitly call him 'king' – he is referred to as a lord/ruler. Nevertheless, 'king' is a reasonable interpretation based on the context.; [minor] The role 'warrior' is somewhat speculative. The Bible describes him primarily as a ruler/tyrant. One might consider adding 'ruler' or 'tyrant' instead of or in addition to 'warrior'.; [major] The final event ('Death of Adoni-Bezek in Jerusalem') states that he died in Jerusalem, but the biblical text in Judges 1:7 says only that he was brought to Jerusalem and died there. The description adds a theological interpretation ('His fate became an example of God's righteous judgment and retribution') which should be distinguished from the narrative account. Furthermore, it is inaccurate to refer only to verse 7 – the event of his being brought to Jerusalem is strictly at the end of verse 7.; [minor] The events 'Adoni-Bezek defeated in battle' and 'Adoni-Bezek's flight and capture' could usefully be combined as they describe a continuous event in verses 5–6. However, splitting them is also acceptable for the level of detail.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile should include interesting historical, linguistic, or theological footnotes, such as on the meaning of the name Adoni-Bezek, the relationship between Adoni-Bezek and Adoni-Zedek, the practice of mutilation in antiquity, and the theological principle of lex talionis (law of retribution).

versions.summary: Adoni-Besek was a Canaanite ruler who reigned in the city of Bezek. He was notorious for his cruelty toward defeated kings – he had cut off the thumbs and big toes of seventy kings who gathered food under his table. After Joshua's death, he was defeated by the tribes of Judah and Simeon, and suffered the same fate he had inflicted on others. Adoni-Besek himself acknowledged that this was God's just retribution, and he was taken to Jerusalem where he died. His story illustrates the biblical principle that God repays people according to their deeds.

versions.reason: [minor] Adoni-Besek was specifically a king/ruler over an area, and his role as 'warrior' is implied but not explicitly described in the text. The title 'king' would have been more precise than 'ruler', given that he himself refers to the 'seventy kings' within his own category. At the same time, it can be argued that 'ruler' is sufficiently comprehensive.; [minor] The description says 'thumbs', but the Hebrew word specifically refers to the thumbs of the hands (not all fingers). The phrasing is acceptable in Norwegian, but 'thumbs' would have been more precise than 'the thumbs'.; [minor] The summary is good, but given that this is version 2 and the previous version scored 6, it should be ensured that the wording is sufficiently distinct and theologically elaborated. The current version is improved, but the last sentence about 'the biblical principle' could have been somewhat more nuanced to avoid becoming too generic.; [minor] The footnote's mention of 'lex talionis' is slightly imprecise. Lex talionis refers specifically to the legal law of retribution ('eye for eye'), whereas what happens to Adoni-Besek can better be described as divine poetic justice or 'middah keneged middah' (measure for measure) in rabbinic terminology. Lex talionis is a legal provision, not a narrative retribution.

versions.summary: Adoni-Besek was a Canaanite ruler who lived in the city of Bezek during the time of Joshua and into the transition to the period of the judges. He was notorious for his brutal treatment of defeated enemies—seventy kings had their thumbs and big toes cut off and were forced to gather food scraps under his table. When the tribes of Judah and Simeon began conquering the territory allotted to them after Joshua's death, Adoni-Besek was defeated and subjected to the same mutilation he had inflicted on others. His own confession—"Seventy kings with cut-off thumbs and big toes gathered food under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me"—serves as a powerful testimony to divine justice. He was then taken to Jerusalem, where he died. The story opens the book of Judges and sets the tone for its themes of God's sovereign intervention and righteous judgment against the wickedness of the Canaanites.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary mentions 'in the time of Joshua and during the transition to the period of the judges,' but Judges 1:1 explicitly states, 'After the death of Joshua.' It is more precise to say that the event took place after Joshua's death, at the beginning of the period of the judges.; [minor] The description says Adoni-Bezek died 'as a result of his injuries and divine retribution.' The biblical text simply states that he died there—the cause is not explicitly specified. It is safer to say that he died there without speculating on the exact cause of death.

footnotes.text: The name 'Adoni-Bezek' likely means 'lord of Bezek' or 'my lord is Bezek.' Some scholars have discussed whether Adoni-Bezek could be identical with Adoni-Zedek, the king of Jerusalem mentioned in Josh 10:1–3, but the names and contexts are sufficiently different that most consider them to be two distinct individuals.

The practice of cutting off thumbs and big toes from defeated enemies is known from the ancient Near East. The purpose was to render the enemy unable to grasp a sword (without a thumb) and to move effectively in battle (without a big toe), thus permanently neutralizing them as warriors.

Adoni-Bezek's acknowledgment of divine retribution reflects the rabbinic principle 'middah keneged middah' (measure for measure), where God repays a person in accordance with their own actions. The fact that a Canaanite ruler himself acknowledges the sovereignty and justice of Israel's God is an important theological point in the introduction to the Book of Judges.

The city of Bezek is traditionally identified with Khirbet Ibziq, about 20 km northeast of Shechem in the central highlands. The site had strategic significance as it controlled important routes between the Jordan Valley and the coastal plain.

In rabbinic tradition, Adoni-Bezek's fate is used as an example that God's justice operates in history—those who practice cruelty will themselves be struck by similar cruelty. Midrash literature draws parallels to other biblical narratives where oppressors meet their own medicine.
